details.title: Blood Circulation
details.scientificExplanation: Blood circulation, described by William Harvey in 1628, transports blood throughout the body via the heart and blood vessels. Blood, composed of water and nutrients, circulates between the spine (sulb) and the ribs (tara'ib), regions associated with the heart and main arteries. This system ensures oxygenation and nutrition of organs.
details.arabicVerse: خُلِقَ مِن مَّاءٍ دَافِقٍ يَخْرُجُ مِن بَيْنِ الصُّلْبِ وَالتَّرَائِبِ
details.verseTranslation: He was created from a gushing fluid, emerging from between the spine and the ribs.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'ma'in dafiq' (gushing fluid) and the location 'sulb wa tara'ib' (spine and ribs) may symbolize blood circulation, corresponding to the modern description of the circulatory system.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, blood circulation was not understood. Harvey's work and modern studies on the heart make the Quranic reference significant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions a gushing fluid between the spine and ribs.
Harvey describes blood circulation.
Discovery of cardiac mechanisms.
Advanced imaging of the circulatory system.

details.title: Cell Division
details.scientificExplanation: Cell division, including mitosis and meiosis, allows for the growth and reproduction of organisms. Discovered by Walther Flemming in 1882, mitosis divides a cell into two identical cells, while meiosis produces gametes for reproduction. These processes are essential for the formation of organisms from a single cell.
details.arabicVerse: خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا
details.verseTranslation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'nafs wahida' (single soul) may symbolize a single cell dividing to form a complex organism, corresponding to cell division processes discovered by modern science.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, cell division mechanisms were unknown. Discoveries in cytology make the Quranic reference relevant.

details.title: DNA Structure
details.scientificExplanation: DNA, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953, is a double helix containing the genetic instructions for life. Formed from a 'nutfah' (drop) like gametes, it encodes traits via nucleotide sequences. Its complexity, with about 3 billion base pairs in humans, reflects a precise design of living organisms.
details.arabicVerse: مِنْ أَيِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ ۖ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ
details.verseTranslation: From what did He create him? From a drop, He created him and gave him his form.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'nutfah' (drop) can symbolize the gametes carrying DNA, and 'faqaddarahu' (gave him his form) reflects genetic programming, corresponding to the complex structure of DNA.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the molecular structure of DNA was unknown. Modern genetic discoveries make the Quranic description significant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions creation from a drop.
Watson and Crick discover the structure of DNA.
Complete sequencing of the human genome.
Advances in gene editing like CRISPR.

diagrams.caption: Illustration of the DNA double helix.

details.title: Immune System
details.scientificExplanation: The immune system protects the body from pathogens via cells like lymphocytes and antibodies. Described by Edward Jenner in the late 18th century with vaccination, it involves innate and adaptive mechanisms. Milk, mentioned in the verse, contains immunoglobulins that strengthen immunity, especially in infants.
details.arabicVerse: وَإِنَّ لَكُمْ فِي الْأَنْعَامِ لَعِبْرَةً
details.verseTranslation: And there is for you, in the cattle, a lesson.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'ibrah' (lesson) can include the benefits of milk, which supports the immune system, corresponding to modern discoveries on immunoglobulins and immune defense.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, immune mechanisms were unknown, though milk was recognized as nourishing. Modern immunological studies make the Quranic reference relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions a lesson in cattle.
Jenner develops the smallpox vaccine.
Discovery of immune mechanisms.
Studies on immunoglobulins in milk.

diagrams.caption: Illustration of the immune system in action.
Diagram of immune cells and antibodies.

details.title: Human Senses
details.scientificExplanation: Sensory organs, such as the eyes, ears, and heart, enable perception and processing of stimuli. Studied by Hermann von Helmholtz in the 19th century, human senses include vision, hearing, and touch, each relying on specialized receptors and complex neural connections.
details.arabicVerse: وَهُوَ الَّذِي أَنشَأَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصَارَ وَالْأَفْئِدَةَ
details.verseTranslation: It is He who has endowed you with hearing, sight, and hearts.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'sam'a' (hearing), 'absar' (sight), and 'af'idah' (hearts) reflect sensory and cognitive organs, corresponding to sensory systems studied in modern neurobiology.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the functions of sensory organs were poorly understood. Modern neuroscientific discoveries make the Quranic description relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the creation of the senses.
Helmholtz studies sensory mechanisms.
Discovery of sensory receptors.
Brain imaging of sensory functions.

details.title: Biological Balance
details.scientificExplanation: Biological balance, or homeostasis, maintains internal conditions of organisms, such as temperature or pH, within viable limits. Described by Claude Bernard in the 19th century, this process involves systems like metabolism and hormonal regulation to ensure the stability of vital functions.
details.arabicVerse: وَالسَّمَاءَ رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ الْمِيزَانَ
details.verseTranslation: He raised the heaven and established the balance.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'mizan' (balance) can symbolize biological homeostasis, corresponding to mechanisms that maintain balance in living organisms.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, homeostasis was unknown. Modern physiological discoveries make the Quranic reference to balance relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the establishment of balance.
Bernard introduces the concept of homeostasis.
Study of biological regulations.
Analysis of complex homeostatic systems.

details.title: Reproductive Systems
details.scientificExplanation: Human reproductive systems, involving male and female gametes, enable the creation of new individuals via fertilization. Described by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the 17th century with the observation of spermatozoa, these systems rely on meiosis and gamete fusion, forming a zygote that develops into an embryo.
details.arabicVerse: خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا
details.verseTranslation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'nafs wahida' (single soul) and 'zawjaha' (its mate) can symbolize the complementarity of male and female gametes, corresponding to reproductive systems described in modern biology.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, reproductive mechanisms were poorly understood. Discoveries in reproductive biology make the Quranic reference relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions creation from a single soul and its mate.
Leeuwenhoek observes spermatozoa.
Study of fertilization mechanisms.
Advances in reproductive biology and IVF.

details.title: Plant Pairs and Genders
details.scientificExplanation: Many plants exhibit male and female characteristics, such as reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) in flowers. Discovered by Carl von Linné in the 18th century, this sexual dimorphism in plants, as in dioecious or monoecious species, enables cross-pollination or self-pollination. For example, corn has distinct male (tassels) and female (ears) flowers.
details.arabicVerse: وَأَنبَتْنَا فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ كَرِيمٍ
details.verseTranslation: And We caused to grow therein all kinds of noble pairs.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'zawj karim' (noble pairs) reflects the male-female duality in plants, corresponding to botanical discoveries on plant reproduction.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, plant reproductive mechanisms were poorly understood. The works of Linné and modern botany make the Quranic description significant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions plant pairs.
Linné classifies plants according to their reproductive organs.
Study of pollination mechanisms.
Genetic analysis of plant genders.

details.title: Photosynthesis Process
details.scientificExplanation: Photosynthesis, described by Jan Ingenhousz in 1779, enables plants to convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen. This process, essential for plant food production, occurs in chloroplasts thanks to chlorophyll. It supports food chains by providing energy to organisms.
details.arabicVerse: هُوَ الَّذِي أَنزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً ۖ لَّكُم مِّنْهُ شَرَابٌ وَمِنْهُ شَجَرٌ فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ
details.verseTranslation: It is He who sends down water from the sky, from which you have drink, and from which grow trees in which you pasture your herds.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'shajar' (trees) and the mention of water from the sky reflect the role of water in photosynthesis, corresponding to modern discoveries on this vital process.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, photosynthesis was unknown. The works of Ingenhousz and modern studies on plant biochemistry make the Quranic description relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions water as a source of plant growth.
Ingenhousz discovers photosynthesis.
Study of chlorophyll mechanisms.
Molecular analysis of photosynthesis.

details.title: Seed Germination
details.scientificExplanation: Seed germination, studied by John Ray in the 17th century, is the process by which a seed becomes a plant through water, oxygen, and adequate temperature. Water activates enzymes, allowing the seed to 'come alive' and grow, as observed in agricultural plants like wheat or corn.
details.arabicVerse: وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنَّكَ تَرَى الْأَرْضَ خَاشِعَةً فَإِذَا أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْهَا الْمَاءَ اهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ
details.verseTranslation: And among His signs is that you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'ihtazzat wa rabat' (stirs and swells) precisely describe water-activated germination, corresponding to biological processes discovered in modern botany.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, germination was observable but poorly understood. Modern botanical studies confirm the Quranic description.

timeline.event: The Quran describes the revitalization of the earth by water.
Ray studies seed germination.
Discovery of enzymes in germination.
Molecular analysis of germination.

details.title: Plant Diversity
details.scientificExplanation: Plant diversity, studied by Carl von Linné in the 18th century, includes thousands of species with varied characteristics, such as grains (habb) and aromatic plants (rayhan). This diversity results from evolution, genetic mutations, and adaptation to environments, such as deserts or tropical forests.
details.arabicVerse: وَالْحَبُّ ذُو الْعَصْفِ وَالرَّيْحَانُ
details.verseTranslation: And the grain with its husk and the fragrant plants.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'habb dhu al-asf' (grain with its husk) and 'rayhan' (fragrant plants) reflect plant diversity, corresponding to modern botanical classification of plant species.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, plant diversity was observable, but its genetic basis was unknown. Modern classifications make the Quranic description relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the variety of plants.
Linné publishes his plant classification.
Genetic study of plant diversity.
Sequencing of plant genomes.

details.title: Pollination Process
details.scientificExplanation: Pollination, studied by Christian Sprengel in 1793, is the transfer of pollen from stamens to pistils, often facilitated by wind (anemophily) or insects. Winds carry pollen from plants like corn or pines, ensuring plant reproduction and seed formation.
details.arabicVerse: وَأَرْسَلْنَا الرِّيَاحَ لَوَاقِحَ
details.verseTranslation: And We sent the winds fertilizing.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'lawaqih' (fertilizing) describes the role of winds in pollination, corresponding to the anemophily process discovered in modern botany.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the role of winds in pollination was unknown. Modern botanical studies confirm the accuracy of the Quranic description.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions fertilizing winds.
Sprengel describes pollination.
Study of anemophily mechanisms.
Analysis of wind-pollen interactions.

details.title: Fruit Formation
details.scientificExplanation: Fruit formation, studied by Joseph Gaertner in the 18th century, follows pollination and fertilization, transforming the flower ovary into a fruit containing seeds. Fruits, such as olives, dates, and grapes mentioned in the verse, are essential for human nutrition and seed dispersal.
details.arabicVerse: يُنبِتُ لَكُم بِهِ الزَّرْعَ وَالزَّيْتُونَ وَالنَّخِيلَ وَالْأَعْنَابَ
details.verseTranslation: He causes to grow for you thereby crops, olives, palm trees, and grapes.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'zar'a' (crops), 'zaytun' (olives), 'nakhil' (palm trees), and 'a'nab' (grapes) reflect fruit formation, corresponding to modern botanical processes of fructification.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, fruit formation was observable, but its biological mechanisms were unknown. Modern botanical studies confirm the Quranic description.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the creation of fruits.
Gaertner publishes his works on fruits.
Study of fructification mechanisms.
Genetic analysis of fruit formation.

details.title: Plant Growth Stages
details.scientificExplanation: Plant growth, studied by Stephen Hales in the 18th century, passes through stages such as germination, vegetative growth, and reproduction. Water, absorbed by roots, supports photosynthesis and nutrient transport, allowing plants to progress from seed to mature plant.
details.arabicVerse: وَهُوَ الَّذِي أَنزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِ نَبَاتَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ
details.verseTranslation: It is He who sends down water from the sky, with which We bring forth the vegetation of all things.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'nabata kulli shay'in' (vegetation of all things) reflects the stages of plant growth, corresponding to biological processes discovered in modern botany.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, plant growth stages were poorly understood. Modern physiological studies make the Quranic description relevant.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions plant growth through water.
Hales publishes his studies on plant physiology.
Discovery of plant hormones.
Molecular analysis of plant growth.

details.title: Medicinal Plants
details.scientificExplanation: Medicinal plants, such as aloe vera or chamomile, produce bioactive compounds with healing properties, studied since antiquity by figures like Hippocrates. Honey, mentioned in the verse, contains antioxidants and antibacterial properties, used to treat infections and wounds.
details.arabicVerse: يَخْرُجُ مِن بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُّخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِّلنَّاسِ
details.verseTranslation: There emerges from their bellies a drink, varying in colors, in which there is healing for people.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'shifa' (healing) reflects the curative properties of honey and plants, corresponding to modern discoveries on plant medicinal compounds.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, medicinal plants were used, but their active compounds were unknown. Modern pharmacological studies confirm the Quranic description.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions healing through a drink.
Hippocrates documents medicinal plants.
Identification of plant bioactive compounds.
Studies on the medicinal properties of honey.

details.title: Vegetation Cycles
details.scientificExplanation: Vegetation cycles, studied by Theophrastus in antiquity and deepened in the 19th century, include germination, growth, flowering, and dormancy. Water, absorbed from the soil, plays a key role in these cycles, allowing plants to complete their life cycle, as in seasonal crops.
details.arabicVerse: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَنزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً فَسَلَكَهُ يَنَابِيعَ فِي الْأَرْضِ
details.verseTranslation: Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky and guides it into springs in the earth?
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'yanabi' fi al-ard' (springs in the earth) reflects the role of water in vegetation cycles, corresponding to modern hydrological and biological processes.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, vegetation cycles were observed, but their mechanisms were poorly understood. Modern studies on plant ecology confirm the Quranic description.

Theophrastus studies plant cycles.

details.title: Tree Structures
details.scientificExplanation: Trees, studied by Theophrastus and deepened by modern dendrology, possess complex structures such as roots, trunks, and leaves. Their growth, supported by the cambium and xylem, allows for the transport of water and nutrients, while their shape reflects adaptation to environments, like pines or palms.
details.arabicVerse: وَالنَّجْمُ وَالشَّجَرُ يَسْجُدَانِ
details.verseTranslation: And the plants and the trees prostrate.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'shajar' (trees) and their 'prostration' can symbolize their functional structure and ecological role, corresponding to modern descriptions of trees.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, trees were recognized, but their internal structures were unknown. Modern dendrological studies make the Quranic description relevant.

Theophrastus describes tree structures.

details.title: Bee Navigation System
details.scientificExplanation: Bees use a sophisticated navigation system based on the sun's position, light polarization, and visual landmarks. Studied by Karl von Frisch in the 1940s, this system includes the 'bee dance' to communicate directions. Bees can also use the Earth's magnetic field for orientation.
details.arabicVerse: فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا
details.verseTranslation: Follow the ways of your Lord, made easy.
details.verseCommentary: The phrase 'subula rabbik dhululan' (ways made easy) reflects the bees' ability to navigate precisely, corresponding to modern discoveries about their orientation.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the mechanisms of bee navigation were unknown. The work of von Frisch and modern ethological studies confirm the accuracy of the Quranic description.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the accessible paths of bees.
Von Frisch discovers the bee dance.

details.title: Ant Communication
details.scientificExplanation: Ants communicate primarily through pheromones, tactile signals, and sometimes sounds, as studied by Edward O. Wilson in the 1960s. For example, they leave chemical trails to indicate paths to food or warn of danger, as in the context of the verse where an ant alerts its peers.
details.arabicVerse: حَتَّىٰ إِذَا أَتَوْا عَلَىٰ وَادِ النَّمْلِ قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَسَاكِنَكُمْ
details.verseTranslation: Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, 'O ants, enter your dwellings.'
details.verseCommentary: The phrase 'qalat namlah' (an ant said) reflects the ability of ants to communicate warnings, corresponding to modern discoveries about pheromones and social communication in insects.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the mechanisms of ant communication were unknown. Modern ethological studies make the Quranic description relevant.

details.title: Bird Flight Patterns
details.scientificExplanation: Birds fly in formation, like geese in a V-shape, to reduce air resistance and save energy, a phenomenon studied by Heinrich Blasius in the early 20th century. These formations, called 'saffat' (in ranks) in the verse, optimize aerodynamics and facilitate communication between birds.
details.arabicVerse: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَن فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالطَّيْرُ صَافَّاتٍ
details.verseTranslation: Do you not see that everyone in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, and the birds with wings outspread?
details.verseCommentary: The term 'saffat' (in ranks) reflects the flight formations of birds, corresponding to modern discoveries about the aerodynamics of avian migration.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, bird flight formations were visible but not scientifically explained. Modern aerodynamic studies confirm the Quranic description.

details.title: Animal Communities
details.scientificExplanation: Many animals, such as bees, ants, and wolves, live in organized communities with defined social roles. Studied by Charles Darwin and others in the 19th century, this social behavior includes cooperation, division of labor, and communication, as in hives or ant colonies.
details.arabicVerse: وَمَا مِن دَابَّةٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا طَائِرٍ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ إِلَّا أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُم
details.verseTranslation: There is no animal on the earth nor a bird that flies with its wings except that they are communities like you.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'umam amthalukum' (communities like you) reflects the social organization of animals, corresponding to modern discoveries in ethology about community structures.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the social behaviors of animals were observed but not explained. Modern ethological studies confirm the Quranic description.

details.title: Spider Webs
details.scientificExplanation: Spider webs, studied by Fritz Vollrath in the 1980s, are fragile yet ingenious structures made of spider silk, a material that is both lightweight and strong. Used to capture prey, these webs are compared in the verse to weak structures, reflecting their fragility against the elements.
details.arabicVerse: مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أَوْلِيَاءَ كَمَثَلِ الْعَنكَبُوتِ اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتًا
details.verseTranslation: The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like that of the spider who takes a home.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'baytan' (home) describes the spider's web, whose fragility symbolizes illusory protections, corresponding to modern observations about web structure.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the structure of spider webs was observable, but their material properties were unknown. Modern studies on spider silk confirm the Quranic description.

details.title: Animal Migration
details.scientificExplanation: Animal migration, studied by Konrad Lorenz in the 1950s, involves seasonal movements guided by environmental signals such as the sun, stars, and the Earth's magnetic field. details.arabicVerse: وَأَوْحَىٰ رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا

Discovery of magnetic navigation mechanisms.

details.title: Honey Production
details.scientificExplanation: Bees produce honey by collecting nectar from flowers, which they transform through regurgitation and evaporation. Studied by Karl von Frisch in the 1940s, honey contains sugars, antioxidants, and antibacterial properties, used as food and remedy since antiquity.
details.arabicVerse: يَخْرُجُ مِن بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُّخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِّلنَّاسِ

details.title: Bird Behavior
details.scientificExplanation: Bird flight is based on aerodynamic principles, such as lift and thrust, studied by Daniel Bernoulli in the 18th century. Birds adjust their wings to glide or flap, allowing stable flight, as described in the verse by 'saffat wa yaqbidn' (wings outspread and folded).
details.arabicVerse: أَلَمْ يَرَوْا إِلَى الطَّيْرِ فَوْقَهُمْ صَافَّاتٍ وَيَقْبِضْنَ
details.verseTranslation: Do they not see the birds above them, with wings outspread and folded?

details.title: Animal Diversity
details.scientificExplanation: Animal diversity, studied by Carl von Linné and Charles Darwin, includes millions of species adapted to different environments. All animals depend on water for their biological processes, as mentioned in the verse, reflecting their common origin in aquatic or humid environments.
details.arabicVerse: وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَ كُلَّ دَابَّةٍ مِّن مَّاءٍ

details.scientificExplanation: The prohibition of consuming impure meat, such as pork or dead animals, reduces the risk of zoonoses and infections, as studied by modern microbiology since Louis Pasteur. These dietary restrictions promote public health.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَيْتَةَ وَالدَّمَ وَلَحْمَ الْخِنزِيرِ
details.verseTranslation: He has only forbidden to you dead animals, blood, and the flesh of swine.
details.verseCommentary: The prohibition of impure foods reflects a preventive measure against diseases, confirmed by modern studies on zoonoses.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, risks associated with impure meat consumption were poorly understood. Quranic prescriptions anticipate modern food safety principles.

timeline.event: The Quran prohibits consumption of impure meat.
Pasteur develops microbiology and pasteurization.
Studies on zoonoses and food safety.

details.title: Sound Therapy
details.scientificExplanation: Sound therapy, studied in the 2000s, uses sound frequencies to reduce stress and improve mental health. The recitation of the Quran, with its rhythmic intonations, can have similar calming effects, as observed in psychophysiological studies.
details.arabicVerse: وَنُنَزِّلُ مِنَ الْقُرْآنِ مَا هُوَ شِفَاءٌ وَرَحْمَةٌ لِّلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
details.verseTranslation: We send down from the Quran that which is healing and mercy for the believers.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'shifa wa rahmah' (healing and mercy) suggests a therapeutic effect of Quranic recitation, corroborated by modern research on sound therapy.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Quranic recitation was a spiritual practice. Modern studies show its beneficial effects on mental health.

details.title: Balanced Nutrition
details.scientificExplanation: A balanced diet, studied by modern dietetics since the work of Wilbur Atwater, includes a variety of foods to provide essential nutrients. The Quran encourages moderate and varied consumption, avoiding excess.
details.arabicVerse: يَا بَنِي آدَمَ خُذُوا زِينَتَكُمْ عِندَ كُلِّ مَسْجِدٍ وَكُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا
details.verseTranslation: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every mosque, eat and drink, but do not be excessive.
details.verseCommentary: The injunction 'kulu wa-shrabu wala tusrifu' (eat and drink without excess) reflects an approach to healthy eating, confirmed by modern nutritional recommendations.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the principles of a balanced diet were not formalized. The Quran anticipates modern concepts of dietary moderation.

timeline.event: The Quran encourages moderate eating.
Atwater develops the foundations of modern dietetics.
Recommendations for a balanced diet.
Studies on varied dietary patterns.

details.title: Sleep and Rest
details.scientificExplanation: Sleep plays a key role in physical and mental recovery, as studied by Nathaniel Kleitman in the 1950s. The Quran describes sleep as 'subat' (rest), corresponding to its role in cellular and cognitive regeneration.
details.arabicVerse: وَهُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا وَالنَّوْمَ سُبَاتًا
details.verseTranslation: It is He who has made the night as a garment and sleep as rest for you.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'subat' (rest) highlights the importance of sleep for health, confirmed by modern research on circadian cycles.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the mechanisms of sleep were unknown. The Quran anticipates modern discoveries about its role in health.

Kleitman discovers REM sleep cycles.

details.title: Stress Management
details.scientificExplanation: Prayer and patience, studied in mindfulness research since the 2000s, reduce stress and improve mental health. The Quran recommends 'sabr wa salah' (patience and prayer) as means of emotional management.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ
details.verseTranslation: O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'ista’inu bis-sabr was-salah' (seek help through patience and prayer) reflects a stress management approach, confirmed by modern studies on mindfulness.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, stress management practices were empirical. The Quran anticipates modern approaches to mental health.

details.title: Addiction Prevention
details.scientificExplanation: Alcohol and gambling, prohibited in the Quran, are associated with mental and physical health disorders, as studied by modern psychiatry. These restrictions reduce the risks of addiction and related diseases, such as cirrhosis or anxiety disorders.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِنَّمَا الْخَمْرُ وَالْمَيْسِرُ وَالْأَنصَابُ وَالْأَزْلَامُ رِجْسٌ مِّنْ عَمَلِ الشَّيْطَانِ
details.verseTranslation: O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling, idolatry, and divining arrows are an abomination, the work of Satan.
details.verseCommentary: The prohibition of 'khamr' (intoxicants) and 'maysir' (gambling) reflects a preventive measure against addictions, confirmed by modern studies on their harmful effects.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the dangers of alcohol and gambling were poorly understood. The Quran anticipates modern discoveries about addictions.

details.title: Benefits of Dates for Pregnancy
details.scientificExplanation: Dates, rich in sugars, iron, and potassium, facilitate uterine contractions and reduce labor time, as shown by studies in 2010. The Quran mentions their consumption by Mary, corresponding to these benefits.
details.arabicVerse: وَهُزِّي إِلَيْكِ بِجِذْعِ النَّخْلَةِ تُسَاقِطْ عَلَيْكِ رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا
details.verseTranslation: Shake the trunk of the palm tree towards you, and it will drop fresh, ripe dates upon you.
details.verseCommentary: The recommendation of dates to Mary reflects their benefits for childbirth, confirmed by modern research on prenatal nutrition.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, dates were a staple food, but their specific effects on childbirth were unknown. Modern studies validate this Quranic prescription.

details.title: Virtues of Olive Oil
details.scientificExplanation: Olive oil, rich in monounsaturated fatty acids and antioxidants, reduces cardiovascular risks, as studied in the 1990s. The Quran describes it as coming from a 'blessed tree,' corresponding to its health benefits.
details.arabicVerse: يُوقَدُ مِن شَجَرَةٍ مُّبَارَكَةٍ زَيْتُونَةٍ لَّا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلَا غَرْبِيَّةٍ
details.verseTranslation: Lit from a blessed tree, an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'shajaratin mubarakatin zaytunah' (blessed tree, an olive tree) reflects the virtues of olive oil, confirmed by modern research on its beneficial effects.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, olive oil was used for lighting and food. Its health benefits are validated by modern science.

details.title: Benefits of Fruits

details.title: Food Hygiene
details.scientificExplanation: The consumption of pure and wholesome foods, as recommended by the Quran, reduces the risk of foodborne illnesses, as studied by modern food safety. The 'tayyibat' (pure) foods correspond to modern standards of food quality.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُلُوا مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ
details.verseTranslation: O you who believe, eat from the good things which We have provided for you.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'tayyibat' (good things) reflects the importance of a healthy diet, confirmed by modern food safety standards.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, concepts of food hygiene were rudimentary. The Quran anticipates modern principles of healthy nutrition.

details.title: Importance of Pure Water
details.scientificExplanation: Pure water is essential for life, as studied by modern biology. It maintains hydration, supports cellular functions, and prevents diseases, as emphasized by the Quran with 'min al-ma'i kulla shay'in hayy' (from water every living thing).
details.arabicVerse: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ
details.verseTranslation: And We made from water every living thing.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'min al-ma'i kulla shay'in hayy' reflects the importance of water for life, confirmed by modern discoveries in biology and hydrology.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the importance of pure water was empirically recognized. The Quran anticipates discoveries about its essential role for health.

details.title: Psychological Balance
details.scientificExplanation: Trust in a spiritual sense, as studied in positive psychology research, reduces anxiety and promotes mental resilience. The Quran describes 'dhikr' (remembrance of God) as a source of tranquility, corresponding to these effects.
details.arabicVerse: الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُم بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ
details.verseTranslation: Those who believe and whose hearts find peace in the remembrance of Allah.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'tatma’inu qulubuhum bidhikr Allah' (hearts find peace in the remembrance of Allah) reflects an anxiety-reduction mechanism, validated by modern psychology.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, spiritual practices were common, but their psychological effects were poorly understood. The Quran anticipates discoveries in mental health.

details.title: Prevention of Excess

details.arabicVerse: وَكُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْرِفِينَ

details.title: Blood Circulation
details.scientificExplanation: The verse alludes to a vital fluid emanating from the body, interpreted as a reference to blood flow. Blood circulation, described by William Harvey in 1628, shows how blood circulates from the heart, echoing the Quranic description of 'maa dafiq' (gushing fluid).
details.arabicVerse: خُلِقَ مِن مَّاءٍ دَافِقٍ يَخْرُجُ مِن بَيْنِ الصُّلْبِ وَالتَّرَائِبِ
details.verseTranslation: He was created from a fluid gushing forth, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'maa dafiq' (gushing fluid) can symbolize blood flow or seminal fluid, reflecting an intuitive understanding of vital processes, corroborated by modern discoveries in circulation.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, blood circulation was not yet scientifically formalized. The Quran uses a metaphorical description that anticipates Harvey's discoveries on the circulatory system.

timeline.event: The Quran alludes to vital flow in the body.

details.title: Brain Function
details.scientificExplanation: The verse mentions the forehead ('nasiya') as the seat of lying, corresponding to the prefrontal cortex, which, according to modern neuroscience (studied by Antonio Damasio in the 1990s), is involved in decision-making and moral behavior.
details.arabicVerse: كَلَّا لَئِن لَّمْ يَنتَهِ لَنَسْفَعًا بِالنَّاصِيَةِ نَاصِيَةٍ كَاذِبَةٍ خَاطِئَةٍ
details.verseTranslation: No! If he does not desist, We will drag him by the forehead, a lying, sinful forehead.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'nasiya kadhiba khati’a' (lying, sinful forehead) reflects an intuitive understanding of the brain's role in behavior, confirmed by modern neuroscience.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, brain functions were poorly understood. The Quran anticipates the role of the prefrontal cortex in complex behaviors.

timeline.event: The Quran associates the forehead with lying.
Damasio studies the prefrontal cortex.
Advances in cognitive neuroscience.
Brain imaging for decision-making.

details.title: Respiration and Oxygen
details.scientificExplanation: The verse describes chest tightness, comparable to breathing difficulty at altitude due to reduced oxygen, studied by respiratory physiology since Joseph Barcroft's work in the early 20th century.
details.arabicVerse: فَمَن يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أَن يَهْدِيَهُ يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَامِ
details.verseTranslation: Whoever Allah wants to guide, He opens his chest to Islam.

details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the effects of altitude on breathing were poorly understood. The Quran uses a metaphor describing this sensation, anticipating scientific discoveries.

details.title: Nervous System
details.scientificExplanation: The verse mentions skin sensitivity to pain, linked to cutaneous nerve endings, studied by modern neurophysiology since Charles Sherrington's work in the early 20th century. The skin contains nociceptive receptors responsible for pain perception.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِآيَاتِنَا سَوْفَ نُصْلِيهِمْ نَارًا كُلَّمَا نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُم بَدَّلْنَاهُمْ جُلُودًا غَيْرَهَا

details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the role of nerve endings in pain was unknown. The Quran anticipates this understanding by describing the skin as a sensitive organ.

details.title: Digestion and Nutrition
details.scientificExplanation: The verse describes milk production from complex digestive processes, reflecting digestion mechanisms studied by William Beaumont in the 19th century. Human digestion, similar to that of animals, transforms nutrients into usable substances like milk.
details.arabicVerse: وَإِنَّ لَكُمْ فِي الْأَنْعَامِ لَعِبْرَةً نُسْقِيكُم مِّمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ مِن بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ وَدَمٍ لَّبَنًا خَالِصًا

details.title: Circadian Rhythms

details.title: Linguistic Challenge
details.scientificExplanation: The verse challenges to produce a text similar to the Quran in style, eloquence, and linguistic structure. Modern literary studies, notably by Angelika Neuwirth on Quranic rhetoric, show that the Quran has a unique structure blending poetry, prose, and rhythm, unmatched in Arabic literature.
details.arabicVerse: وَإِن كُنتُمْ فِي رَيْبٍ مِّمَّا نَزَّلْنَا عَلَىٰ عَبْدِنَا فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِّن مِّثْلِهِ
details.verseTranslation: And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our Servant, then produce a surah like it.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'surah min mithlihi' (a surah like it) highlights the linguistic inimitability of the Quran, a challenge never met according to literary scholars.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Arabic poetry was at its peak, but no poet succeeded in producing a text comparable to the Quran, reinforcing its unique character.

details.title: Scientific Challenge
details.scientificExplanation: The verse states that the heavens and earth were joined before being separated, evoking a description compatible with the Big Bang, theorized by Georges Lemaître in 1927. This invitation to reflect on creation challenges pre-modern scientific conceptions.
details.arabicVerse: أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَنَّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ كَانَتَا رَتْقًا فَفَتَقْنَاهُمَا

details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, cosmological theories were limited. The Quran anticipates the notion of cosmic expansion with remarkable precision.

details.title: Historical Challenge

details.arabicVerse: غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ فِي أَدْنَى الْأَرْضِ وَهُم مِّن بَعْدِ غَلَبِهِمْ سَيَغْلِبُونَ
details.verseTranslation: The Romans have been defeated in the lowest land, but they, after their defeat, will overcome.
details.verseCommentary: The expression 'sayaghlubun' (they will overcome) reflects a precise prediction, confirmed by historical events, reinforcing the prophetic character of the Quran.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the prediction of Roman victory was bold, as the Byzantines were in a weak position. The Quran anticipates this event with precision.

details.title: Miracle of Moses Parting the Sea
details.scientificExplanation: The account of Moses parting the sea is often considered a miraculous event defying natural laws. However, some scientific hypotheses propose that natural phenomena, such as strong winds or tsunamis, could have created temporary passages in shallow seas, like the Red Sea. For example, computer simulations (2010) showed that strong winds blowing for several hours could push back water under certain geographical conditions. While these explanations do not confirm the account, they suggest possible natural mechanisms that could have been amplified by divine timing.
details.arabicVerse: فَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ أَنِ اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ ۖ فَانفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ
details.verseTranslation: We inspired Moses: 'Strike the sea with your staff.' It parted, and each part became like a great mountain.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'falaqa' (parted) and the description of the sea parts as 'mountains' highlight a spectacular event where water separated to create a passage. This miracle is presented as a divine intervention to save Moses and his people from oppression.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, miracle accounts were common in religious traditions, but the precise description of a sea splitting into two distinct parts, like 'mountains,' is unique in its clarity. This Quranic account aligns with biblical traditions, but its narrative precision is remarkable for the time.

timeline.event: The Quran describes the miracle of Moses parting the sea.

details.title: Miracle of Moses' Staff Turning into a Serpent
details.scientificExplanation: The transformation of Moses' staff into a serpent is described as a miracle defying natural laws. details.arabicVerse: فَأَلْقَىٰ عَصَاهُ فَإِذَا هِيَ ثُعْبَانٌ مُّبِينٌ

details.title: Miracle of Jesus Healing the Blind
details.scientificExplanation: The healing of the blind and lepers, attributed to Jesus, is regarded as a miracle. Modern medicine notes that certain forms of blindness, such as those caused by infections or deficiencies, can be reversible with treatments. However, the instantaneous healing described in the Quran exceeds current medical capabilities, suggesting divine intervention. Accounts of miraculous healings may also have a psychological impact, strengthening the faith of witnesses.
details.arabicVerse: وَتُبْرِئُ الْأَكْمَهَ وَالْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِي
details.verseTranslation: And you heal the blind from birth and the leper by My permission.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'akmah' (blind from birth) indicates healing of congenital conditions, an exceptional feat. The phrase 'by My permission' emphasizes that these miracles are divine acts performed through Jesus.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, accounts of miraculous healings were widespread in Christian and Jewish traditions. The Quran's specificity regarding the healing of the blind from birth and lepers reflects detailed knowledge of these traditions, reinforcing Jesus' role as a prophet.

details.title: Miracle of Jesus Speaking in the Cradle
details.scientificExplanation: The miracle of Jesus speaking in the cradle defies any scientific explanation, as infants lack the physical capacity to speak. This phenomenon is regarded as divine intervention, serving to defend Mary against accusations and affirm Jesus' prophetic mission from birth.
details.arabicVerse: فَأَشَارَتْ إِلَيْهِ ۖ قَالُوا كَيْفَ نُكَلِّمُ مَن كَانَ فِي الْمَهْدِ صَبِيًّا ۝ قَالَ إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ
details.verseTranslation: She pointed to him. They said: 'How can we speak to one who is a child in the cradle?' He said: 'I am the servant of Allah.'
details.verseCommentary: This verse highlights Jesus' miraculous ability to speak from a very young age, a clear sign of his divine mission. This event aims to protect Mary's honor and confirm the truth of his prophethood.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, apocryphal Christian accounts, such as the Infancy Gospel, mentioned similar childhood miracles of Jesus. The Quran incorporates this miracle in a unique context, emphasizing the defense of Mary and prophetic confirmation.

details.title: Miracle of Muhammad's Night Journey
details.scientificExplanation: The Night Journey (Isra) and Ascension (Mi'raj) are supernatural events with no direct scientific explanation. Some researchers suggest a spiritual or visionary experience, while Islamic tradition supports a physical miraculous journey. The speed of the journey from Mecca to Jerusalem in one night defies 7th-century physical limitations, highlighting its miraculous nature.
details.arabicVerse: سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِّنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى

details.verseCommentary: The term 'asra' (took by night) indicates a miraculous journey. This verse highlights the connection between holy sites and Muhammad's prophetic mission, reinforcing his universal role.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, a journey from Mecca to Jerusalem took weeks. The Quranic description of a one-night journey was inconceivable without divine intervention, strengthening the faith of early Muslims against skeptics.

details.title: Miracle of the Splitting of the Moon
details.scientificExplanation: The splitting of the moon is a miracle with no direct scientific explanation. details.title: Miracle of Noah and the Ark

details.title: Pharaoh's Death by Drowning
details.scientificExplanation: Pharaoh's drowning is a theological narrative with no definitive archaeological proof. Some speculate it relates to the mummified body of Ramses II, though unconfirmed. The preservation of the body is seen in the Quran as a divine sign, emphasizing divine justice.
details.arabicVerse: حَتَّىٰ إِذَا أَدْرَكَهُ الْغَرَقُ قَالَ آمَنتُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا الَّذِي آمَنَتْ بِهِ بَنُو إِسْرَائِيلَ
details.verseTranslation: When drowning overtook him, he said: 'I believe there is no deity except Him in whom the Children of Israel believe.'
details.verseCommentary: The term 'gharaq' (drowning) illustrates divine punishment for Pharaoh's arrogance. His late repentance is rejected, showing that faith under duress is not accepted.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, this narrative reinforced belief in divine justice against tyrants, resonating with early Muslims' struggles against oppression.

timeline.event: Presumed drowning of Pharaoh according to religious narratives.
The Quran recounts Pharaoh's drowning as divine punishment.
Discovery of Egyptian mummies, speculation on Quranic connection.

details.title: Brain of the Heart
details.scientificExplanation: The Quran uses the heart as a metaphor for understanding, while modern neuroscience attributes cognition to the brain. Recent studies show heart-brain interaction via the nervous system, influencing emotions and decision-making, reflecting an ancient intuitive understanding.
details.arabicVerse: أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَتَكُونَ لَهُمْ قُلُوبٌ يَعْقِلُونَ بِهَا
details.verseTranslation: Have they not traveled through the land so they may have hearts with which they understand?
details.verseCommentary: The term 'qulub' (hearts) symbolizes consciousness and reason. The verse critiques spiritual blindness, encouraging reflection on divine signs through the 'heart.'
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, the heart was seen as the seat of thought in many cultures. The Quran adapted this belief to promote spiritual reflection.

timeline.event: The Quran describes the heart as the seat of understanding.
Discovery of the brain's role in cognition.
Research on heart-brain interaction.

details.title: Fly Possessing a Remedy
details.scientificExplanation: This verse is often linked to a hadith where the Prophet mentions a remedy in a fly's wing. Modern science explores antimicrobial properties in fly secretions, though medical applications remain experimental.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ ضُرِبَ مَثَلٌ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ ۚ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ لَن يَخْلُقُوا ذُبَابًا
details.verseTranslation: O people, a parable is presented, so listen: those you invoke besides Allah cannot create a fly.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'dhubab' (fly) illustrates the idols' inability to create even an insignificant creature, emphasizing unique divine power.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, flies were seen as pests. The Quran uses this example to challenge polytheistic beliefs and encourage reflection on divine creation.

timeline.event: The Quran uses the fly as a parable.
Research on insect biological properties.
Studies on antimicrobial compounds in flies.

details.title: Animal on the Back of a Mosquito
details.scientificExplanation: The verse mentions the 'mosquito' and 'what is above it,' possibly symbolizing microscopic creatures like parasites carried by mosquitoes. Modern microbiology confirms the complexity of microscopic ecosystems, reflecting divine precision.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَسْتَحْيِي أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلًا مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا
details.verseTranslation: Allah does not shy away from using the example of a mosquito or what is above it.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'ba'uda' (mosquito) and 'ma fawqaha' (what is above it) show that even the smallest creatures reflect divine greatness, challenging skeptics' mockery.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, small creatures were often despised. The Quran uses this example to illustrate the perfection of divine creation, even in the insignificant.

timeline.event: The Quran uses the mosquito as a parable.
Invention of the microscope, revealing microscopic organisms.
Studies on parasites carried by mosquitoes.

details.title: Female Anopheles Mosquito and Its Bite
details.scientificExplanation: The female Anopheles mosquito is known to transmit malaria through its bite. The Quran uses the mosquito as an example of divine complexity, confirmed by modern science through studies of its ecological and biological role.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَسْتَحْيِي أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلًا مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا
details.verseTranslation: Allah does not shy away from using the example of a mosquito or what is above it.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'ba'uda' (mosquito) symbolizes divine precision in creation, even for an apparently insignificant creature, challenging skeptics of the time.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, mosquitoes were seen as nuisances. The Quran uses them to illustrate divine perfection in the smallest details of creation.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions the mosquito as a parable.
Discovery of Anopheles' role in malaria transmission.
Research on mosquitoes and their ecological impact.

details.title: Source of Buried Minerals
details.scientificExplanation: The Quran mentions gold and precious stones as treasures, reflecting geological processes of mineral formation in the Earth's crust. Modern geology explains that gold and diamonds form under extreme pressure and temperature.
details.arabicVerse: لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ عَدْنٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهِمُ الْأَنْهَارُ يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيهَا مِنْ أَسَاوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ
details.verseTranslation: They will have gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow, adorned therein with bracelets of gold.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'dhahab' (gold) symbolizes wealth and beauty in Paradise, but also reflects the value of earthly minerals, emphasizing divine creation.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, gold and gems symbolized wealth. The Quran uses them to describe Paradise while pointing to their earthly origin.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions gold as a symbol of divine reward.
Beginning of modern geological studies on mineral formation.
Advances in extraction and analysis of precious minerals.

details.title: Wisdom of David
details.scientificExplanation: David's wisdom is a theological concept. Modern psychology studies decision-making and justice, but 'divine wisdom' transcends scientific explanation. The Quran presents David as a model of fair judgment.
details.arabicVerse: وَشَدَدْنَا مُلْكَهُ وَآتَيْنَاهُ الْحِكْمَةَ وَفَصْلَ الْخِطَابِ
details.verseTranslation: We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'hikma' (wisdom) and 'fasl al-khitab' (decisive speech) highlight David's ability to judge fairly, reflecting divine guidance.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, prophetic stories like David's inspired Muslims to seek justice and wisdom in their judgments.

timeline.event: Presumed reign of David according to religious traditions.
The Quran describes David as a wise prophet.
Comparative studies on prophetic figures.

details.title: Wisdom of Solomon
details.scientificExplanation: Solomon's wisdom is a theological concept with no direct scientific equivalent. Modern psychology studies wisdom as a blend of knowledge and judgment, but the Quran attributes Solomon's wisdom to divine inspiration.
details.arabicVerse: وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا دَاوُودَ وَسُلَيْمَانَ عِلْمًا ۖ وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنَا
details.verseTranslation: We gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said: 'Praise be to Allah who favored us.'
details.verseCommentary: The term 'ilm' (knowledge) denotes divine knowledge granted to Solomon, enabling him to understand creation and judge fairly.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Solomon's stories inspired Muslims to seek knowledge and wisdom, linked to piety and gratitude toward God.

timeline.event: Presumed reign of Solomon according to religious traditions.
The Quran describes Solomon as a knowledgeable prophet.
Studies on prophetic figures across religions.

details.title: Divine Assistance to Noah
details.scientificExplanation: The story of Noah's Ark is theological with no direct scientific equivalent. However, major ancient floods, such as those in the Mediterranean basin, may have inspired this universal narrative found in several traditions.
details.arabicVerse: وَاصْنَعِ الْفُلْكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا
details.verseTranslation: Build the ark under Our eyes and Our inspiration.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'fulk' (ark) and 'a'yunina' (Our eyes) emphasize direct divine assistance in building the ark, symbolizing God's protection for the righteous.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Noah's story illustrated divine mercy for believers and punishment for disbelievers, strengthening the faith of early Muslims.

timeline.event: Flood narratives in various traditions.
The Quran recounts divine assistance to Noah.
Archaeological research on ancient floods.

details.title: Divine Assistance to Muhammad
details.scientificExplanation: Divine assistance to Muhammad is a theological concept. Psychology may interpret these experiences as moments of resilience amid trials, but the Quran attributes them to direct divine intervention.
details.arabicVerse: أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَىٰ ۝ وَوَجَدَكَ ضَالًّا فَهَدَىٰ ۝ وَوَجَدَكَ عَائِلًا فَأَغْنَىٰ
details.verseTranslation: Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? Did He not find you lost and guide you? Did He not find you in need and enrich you?
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'yatim' (orphan), 'dallan' (lost), and 'a'ilan' (in need) describe Muhammad's trials, while 'awa', 'hada', and 'aghna' show divine assistance at each stage.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Muhammad faced personal and social trials. This verse consoled early Muslims by showing God supports His prophets.

timeline.event: Birth and trials of Muhammad.
Revelation of Surah Ad-Duha to comfort Muhammad.
Studies on prophetic biography.

details.title: Virtue of Prayer
details.scientificExplanation: Prayer is a spiritual act, but studies in psychology show that meditative practices, like prayer, reduce stress and improve mental well-being, which may reflect the benefits of the spiritual connection described in the Quran.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ
details.verseTranslation: O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'sala' (prayer) and 'sabr' (patience) emphasize that prayer is a means of spiritual and emotional resilience in the face of trials.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, prayer was a central pillar of nascent Islam, providing Muslims with a way to strengthen their faith and community in the face of persecution.

timeline.event: The Quran establishes prayer as a pillar of faith.
Studies on the psychological effects of prayer.
Research on meditation and mental well-being.

details.title: Benefits of Charity
details.scientificExplanation: Charity is an act of kindness that, according to psychology, promotes well-being by enhancing empathy and social connection. The Quran presents charity as a means of purifying the soul and multiplying spiritual rewards.
details.arabicVerse: مَّثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَالَهُمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أَنبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنَابِلَ
details.verseTranslation: The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed that produces seven spikes.
details.verseCommentary: The metaphor of the 'seed' illustrates the multiplication of charity rewards, highlighting its spiritual and social impact.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, charity (zakat) was a pillar of Islam, aimed at reducing social inequalities in a often tribal society.

timeline.event: The Quran establishes charity as a religious duty.
Studies on the social impact of charity.
Research on the psychological effects of altruism.

details.title: Preservation of Chastity
details.scientificExplanation: Chastity, as described in the Quran, promotes personal discipline. Psychology shows that self-control strengthens mental health and social relationships, aligning chastity with social and spiritual benefits.
details.arabicVerse: قُل لِّلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ وَيَحْفَظُوا فُرُوجَهُمْ
details.verseTranslation: Tell the believers to lower their gaze and preserve their chastity.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'yaghuddu' (lower their gaze) and 'yahfazu furujahum' (preserve their chastity) emphasize moral discipline as a means of preserving dignity.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Arab society had varying standards of morality. The Quran introduced strict chastity rules to promote honor and ethics.

timeline.event: The Quran commands chastity as a virtue.
Studies on the impact of moral discipline.
Research on chastity and mental health.

details.title: Obedience to Parents
details.scientificExplanation: Respect for parents, as promoted in the Quran, strengthens family ties. Psychology shows that positive family relationships reduce stress and promote social cohesion.
details.arabicVerse: وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا
details.verseTranslation: Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him and that you be kind to your parents.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'ihsan' (kindness) implies respectful and generous treatment of parents, linking this duty to piety toward God.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Arab society valued tribal ties, but the Quran emphasized the nuclear family, promoting kindness to parents as a spiritual duty.

timeline.event: The Quran commands kindness toward parents.
Studies on the impact of family relationships.
Research on family resilience.

details.title: Prayer as Protection Against Evil
details.scientificExplanation: Prayer, according to psychology, promotes mental discipline and reduces anxiety, offering psychological protection. The Quran links this act to preventing reprehensible behaviors, strengthening morality.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ الصَّلَاةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنكَرِ
details.verseTranslation: Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'tanha' (prohibits) indicates that prayer acts as a spiritual shield, reinforcing moral discipline and connection with God.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, prayer was a means of strengthening Muslim resilience against moral and social challenges of the time.

timeline.event: The Quran links prayer to morality.
Studies on the effects of prayer on behavior.
Research on prayer and mental health.

details.title: Charity as Purification
details.scientificExplanation: Charity promotes altruism, which, according to psychology, improves mental and social well-being. The Quran presents charity as a means of purifying the soul and wealth, reinforcing social responsibility.
details.arabicVerse: خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم بِهَا
details.verseTranslation: Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them increase.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'sadaqa' (charity) and 'tutahhiruhum' (purify them) highlight the spiritual and social role of charity, purifying both the individual and the community.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, charity was a key mechanism for reducing inequalities in a society often marked by economic disparities.

timeline.event: The Quran establishes charity as purification.
Studies on the economic impact of charity.
Research on altruism and positive psychology.

details.title: Chastity as Honor
details.scientificExplanation: Chastity promotes personal discipline, which psychology associates with better mental health and stable social relationships. The Quran links chastity to honor and morality, reinforcing individual dignity.
details.arabicVerse: وَقُل لِّلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِنَّ وَيَحْفَظْنَ فُرُوجَهُنَّ
details.verseTranslation: And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their chastity.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'yaghdudna' (lower their gaze) and 'yahfazna furujahunna' (guard their chastity) emphasize morality and the protection of women's honor.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, standards of modesty varied. The Quran established clear rules to promote chastity as a universal value in the Muslim community.

timeline.event: The Quran commands chastity for women.
Studies on modesty and morality in societies.
Research on the impact of moral discipline.

details.title: Respect for Parents as an Act of Piety
details.scientificExplanation: Respect for parents strengthens family ties, which psychology associates with better mental health and social cohesion. Studies show that positive family relationships reduce stress and promote emotional well-being.
details.arabicVerse: وَوَصَّيْنَا الْإِنسَانَ بِوَالِدَيْهِ حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ
details.verseTranslation: And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents. His mother carried him, [increasing her] in weakness upon weakness.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'wahn' (weakness) highlights maternal sacrifices, reinforcing the moral obligation to respect parents as an act of piety linked to gratitude toward God.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, in a tribal society, the Quran emphasized the nuclear family, promoting respect for parents as an essential spiritual virtue.

timeline.event: The Quran commands kindness toward parents.
Studies on the importance of family relationships for mental health.

details.title: Prayer for Divine Guidance
details.scientificExplanation: Prayer for guidance, as in Al-Fatihah, can be seen as a meditative practice. Psychology shows that repetitive prayers promote focus and reduce anxiety, strengthening the sense of spiritual connection.
details.arabicVerse: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ ۝ صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ
details.verseTranslation: Guide us to the straight path—the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'sirat al-mustaqim' (straight path) symbolizes a life aligned with divine values. This prayer, recited daily, reinforces the quest for moral and spiritual guidance.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Al-Fatihah was at the heart of Muslim prayers, serving as a spiritual guide for believers in a context of social and religious challenges.

timeline.event: Revelation of Surah Al-Fatihah, a pillar of Muslim prayers.
Studies on the effects of meditative practices like prayer.
Research on prayer and mental health.

details.title: Charity to Support the Needy
details.scientificExplanation: Charity promotes altruism, which psychology associates with improved well-being and social cohesion. The Quran presents charity as a means of supporting the poor, strengthening community solidarity.
details.arabicVerse: وَآتَى الْمَالَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ ذَوِي الْقُرْبَىٰ وَالْيَتَامَىٰ وَالْمَسَاكِينَ
details.verseTranslation: And gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy.
details.verseCommentary: The terms 'ata al-mal' (gives wealth) and 'ala hubbih' (in spite of love for it) emphasize selfless generosity, an act that purifies the soul and strengthens the community.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, charity was essential for reducing inequalities in a tribal society. The Quran institutionalized charity as a spiritual and social duty.

timeline.event: The Quran promotes charity as an act of piety.

Research on altruism and community cohesion.

details.title: Preservation of Pharaoh's Body
details.scientificExplanation: The Quran mentions the preservation of Pharaoh's body as a sign. Some speculations associate this with Egyptian mummies, such as that of Ramses II, although without conclusive archaeological evidence. Egyptian mummification, practiced for millennia, reflects advanced preservation techniques.
details.arabicVerse: فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً
details.verseTranslation: So today We will save your body that you may be a sign for those after you.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'badanik' (your body) emphasizes the physical preservation of Pharaoh as a divine sign, intended to inspire reflection for future generations.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, this verse served to reinforce belief in divine signs, contrasting with Pharaoh's arrogance towards Moses.

timeline.event: Presumed drowning of Pharaoh and preservation of his body.
The Quran mentions the preservation of Pharaoh's body.
Discovery of Egyptian mummies, speculations about their connection to the Quran.

details.title: Number of Days in a Year
details.scientificExplanation: The word 'yawm' (day) appears 365 times in the Quran, corresponding to the number of days in a solar year. This coincidence is often interpreted as a numerical harmony, although the solar year is not explicitly mentioned in the Quran.
details.arabicVerse: وَلَبِثُوا فِي كَهْفِهِمْ ثَلَاثَ مِائَةٍ سِنِينَ وَازْدَادُوا تِسْعًا
details.verseTranslation: And they remained in their cave for three hundred years and added nine.
details.verseCommentary: This verse refers to the People of the Cave, where the period of 309 years (300 + 9) may symbolize a significant duration, although the connection with 365 days is a textual observation rather than contextual.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, lunar calendars dominated Arabia. The observation of the number 365 is a modern analysis, highlighting the perceived precision of the Quranic text.

timeline.event: The Quran uses the word 'yawm' 365 times.
Studies on numerical patterns in the Quran.
Analysis of textual coincidences such as the number 365.

details.title: Number of Months in a Year
details.scientificExplanation: The word 'shahr' (month) appears 12 times in the Quran, corresponding to the number of months in a lunar year. This verse explicitly establishes the 12 months, aligned with the Islamic lunar calendar.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ عِدَّةَ الشُّهُورِ عِندَ اللَّهِ اثْنَا عَشَرَ شَهْرًا
details.verseTranslation: Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'ithna ashara' (twelve) confirms the Islamic lunar calendar, structuring time for religious rituals such as fasting and pilgrimage.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Arabs used a luni-solar calendar. This verse standardized the lunar calendar for the Muslim community.

timeline.event: The Quran establishes the 12 months of the lunar year.
Studies on Islamic calendars.
Analysis of numerical patterns in the Quranic text.

details.title: Balance Between Man and Woman
details.scientificExplanation: The words 'rajul' (man) and 'imra'ah' (woman) each appear 24 times, suggesting symbolic balance. Although not related to biology, this balance reflects spiritual equality in the Quranic text.
details.arabicVerse: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ
details.verseTranslation: O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from a single soul.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'nafs wahida' (single soul) emphasizes the common origin of humanity, men and women, reinforcing the idea of equality in divine creation.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, Arab society was patriarchal. This verse promotes a vision of spiritual equality between men and women.

timeline.event: The Quran establishes spiritual equality between men and women.
Studies on textual patterns in the Quran.
Analysis of equality concepts in religious texts.

details.title: Jesus and Adam Mentioned Equally
details.scientificExplanation: The names 'Isa' (Jesus) and 'Adam' each appear 25 times, reflecting their similarity in divine creation without biological parents (Adam without parents, Jesus without a father). This textual coincidence is a modern observation, with no direct link to science.
details.arabicVerse: إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ
details.verseTranslation: Indeed, the example of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'mathal' (example) compares the miraculous creation of Jesus to that of Adam, emphasizing the uniqueness of divine power.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, this verse addressed theological debates with Christians, affirming Jesus' human nature while recognizing his miracle.

timeline.event: The Quran compares Jesus and Adam.
Studies on numerical patterns in the Quran.
Analysis of comparative prophetic narratives.

details.title: Angels and Demons in Balance
details.scientificExplanation: The words 'mala'ika' (angels) and 'shayatin' (demons) each appear 88 times, suggesting symbolic balance between good and evil. This textual observation has no direct scientific correlation but reflects an intentional literary structure.
details.arabicVerse: وَاتَّبَعُوا مَا تَتْلُو الشَّيَاطِينُ عَلَىٰ مُلْكِ سُلَيْمَانَ
details.verseTranslation: And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon.
details.verseCommentary: The term 'shayatin' (demons) contrasts with angels, illustrating the duality between divine guidance and temptation in the Quran.
details.historicalContext: In the 7th century, belief in angels and demons was widespread. The Quran uses this duality to teach morality and responsibility.

timeline.event: The Quran mentions angels and demons in balance.
Studies on textual patterns in the Quran.
Analysis of dualities in religious texts.

details.title: Life and Death Balanced
details.scientificExplanation: The words 'hayat' (life) and 'mawt' (death) each appear 145 times, symbolizing the balance between these two states. Biology studies life and death, but this textual balance is a literary observation with no direct scientific link.
details.arabicVerse: الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْمَوْتَ وَالْحَيَاةَ لِيَبْلُوَكُمْ
details.verseTranslation: He who created death and life to test you.
